I'll admit it. I am an audio nerd. I worked professionally as an Audio/Video Engineer for a number of years, and had the opportunity to use some very refined equipment in the process. I don't believe my hearing is more sensitive than anyone else's (It might be worse truth be told), but I can get picky when it comes to audio of any sort. Every system I use has to be calibrated just right. That pickiness has carried over to headphones, and as a vmoda user for 5 years running, I have always been impressed by how their sound compares to much more expensive options. The quality of the sound is great, whether you are a newbie to headphones, or someone who cares quite a bit. They have powerful lows, wide mids, and super clear highs. Instead of the bass heavy headphones that are currently the trend, these actually let you hear the rest of the song, and in just as sharp detail. And the sound just gets better as you wear them in. Having had a pair of V-80s previously, and using their immortal life program, I upgraded to these XS ON-Ears. While the sound is very similar, there are definitely some improvements, especially in the highs and to a lesser extent, the mids. They are even less muddled than before, and the range is much wider. For the price, there isn't really anything else out there that blows these away in the sound department. Moving on, the build on these things is topnotch. They look, feel, and weigh premium, and the materials they use just accentuate that fact. The customizable ear plates are an awesome touch if you like to have a unique look, and there is a vast range of customization, at widely ranging price points. Having had a pair of V-80s for years, I can tell you that these things are durable. I have hiked, camped, gone biking, running, and rock climbing with them on and they survived some falls with no problems. The XS are no different in toughness or quality. And if anything were to happen regarding a malfunction,or breaking when it shouldn't(as outlined in their warranty) they are great with getting you taken care of and back to the music. Did I mention that they sit very close to your head and are super low profile for when it comes to having a hood on? For storage, they fold down super small, almost too small at first. I would recommend these to anyone asking me for a nice pair of on-ear headphones, without worrying about them, or my reputation. Go ahead and click that order button.

I don't write a lot of reviews but I felt compelled to write one here because I have strong feelings about these headphones. Let me start by saying that I am I generally a fan of Bose. I used the QC 20 earbuds every day for years until they fell apart and I absolutely loved them. Then I switched to the QC 35 which are the best headphones I've ever owned. These headphones sound great, the Bluetooth works very well, and I have no issues with the battery life. As just a pair of earbuds, they are pretty good. However, there are two major drawbacks which make them very disappointing and important enough to say I would not recommend them. First, they are simply not comfortable. The bulkiness and weight of the ear pieces are simply uncomfortable and after dozens of runs and hours of use, I simply don't like wearing them. I always found the ear tips of the QC 20's to be super comfortable - I could wear them for 6-8 hours without even thinking about them. But I really don't like wearing the SoundSports. Second, the volume/mic piece is a massive design flaw. It's so heavy that it constantly pulls the cable to one side. If you were simply sitting at your desk or on a train, this wouldn't be an issue. But for running headphones, this is completely unacceptable. If I am wearing a hat or headband, I will pull the cable through it to try and keep it in place. Otherwise, I'm constantly pulling at it to straighten it out and when you're exercising, the last thing you want to be focusing on is your equipment. I absolutely loved my QC20's and still love my 35's, but these SoundSport headphones are a miss. I'm still high on Bose, but if you're looking for comfortable bluetooth headphones for running, I'd pass on these.

These sound amazing and give crystal clear wireless performance with an open back design. The plush ear cushions feel very comfortable, even with long listening sessions. The top band also has two cushions that sit the phones comfortably on the vertex of the head--so much that it's hardly noticeable. The speakers do not twirl like a DJ set, which I like because they are easier to set down and handle without things flopping all over the place. The plastic body is hard and higher quality than typical headphones. These things can take a beating and still look like new! The only thing I don't like about these is the design of the power (mostly) and volume controls. To turn them on, after removing from the base, you have to hold down the small power until a green light turns on, there is a slight delay, and the audio plays. It sounds fine, but in practicality there is no tactile feedback in the button or tone to let you know they are on, only a green light. Basically, there is no clear fast reliable way to turn these on without waiting a few seconds watching the light and holding the button, which means many times I've been caught in a cycle of on-off if I put them on first and try to turn on based on feel. I swear sometimes I'll hold it and they won't turn on, I'll hold again and then it will turn off right after turning on. There is also a delay after taking them off the base before they will turn on, making it even more of a hassle if I'm moving fast. It might not sound like much of an issue but I'd much rather have a different design, like a slide switch. I occasionally use the volume buttons when I have to but try not to because they are all so close together with the fase buttons. I'd prefer different shaped buttons or a wheel for better control. My center balance button doesn't seem to work but I don't care about that. The only other thing that is annoying is that the bands leading to the top are a bit loose, so the speakers tend to drop low and long over time. All in all, I love these, there are just a few annoyances that can be fixed for later models. (I use these for computer gaming using optical audio out.)

The problem with them is that they aren't long enough (don't fit deeply enough into the ear) to be very comfortable. The edge of the bud sort of scrapes in the ear a bit. It's soft silicone so it isn't painful, just not especially comfortable. The audio quality is fine, but the microphone is pretty much unusable. People I have spoken with using these headphones tell me they can't hear me or that I sound like I'm at the end of a long tunnel. They're completely unusable in a car. The ear buds are touch sensitive on the flat surface that sticks out of the ear. The entire surface is sensitive, which makes it annoying when you want to push the earbud more securely in your ear and it turns off your music or skips a track. My final complaint with these buds is that you need the box to pair it with your phone. If the buds time-out from being not used for a few minutes the only way to re-enable them is to put them back in the box for a moment and take them back out. I'd try a different brand if I know about them what I do now.

The 19-year-old gear-head audiophile in the house recommended I look a the Monoprice 560's. Specs looked good and having a set of planar headphones appealed to the geek in me. Unboxing was nice with a good looking inner package and nice presentation of the phones upon opening. I was a little surprised to see individual connections for each side, but I guess it makes for better durability and possible ease of replacement if something gets busted. I plugged them into my workstation PC and went to one of my reference pieces of music -- the 1964 live recording of Dave Brubeck doing "Take Five". The Sound The presence and clarity let me hear things that I had not noticed before. A little scratchiness in the sax, a bit of staccato off the cymbles, and an overall precision I didn't get even with my Etymotics. Adding an amp between the workstation and the headphones was even more fun and let me push it to the point of silliness. A little harsh at first compare to my much less expensive and technically advanced sets, but they simply show what is there. I moved over to the CBS Masterworks version of Pachabel's Canon and was equally pleased. The Build These are rock solid and kind of innovative. The backs pop off to allow a selection between Open and Closed cups. The ear pads are also magnetically connected and have alignment pins, so that pad replacement should be a snap. The bridge bar appears to be spring steel (which leads to an issue noted below) and should last a lifetime. The cups are solid as well and feel bomb proof. My Issue: Because the headband appears to be Spring Steel and it is acoustically coupled to the cups, even the slightest rub on the bar is clearly hears/ It also adds more than a bit to the weight. Given the sound, build quality and price point, these are damn fine for less than $500. PROS: - Great initial sound - Solid Build - Pleasing to look at - Great price Point CONS: - A tad heavy - Contact noise transfer from the headband to the cups - No instructions or marketing Bladi Blasi - Very fancy packaging that just gets tossed. Overall I'm happy and would buy them again. No remorse at all.

These open-back cans are one of the best pairs of headphones I've ever used. With massive and beautifully accurate soundstage, these cans are perfect for listening to most types of music, and, when combined with an in-line microphone, they make an excellent gaming headset. The Perfect: - The open-back nature of this line of headphones provides a much more "roomy" and open listening experience. That is, these headphones emulate the sound of a large room or auditorium much better than, say, the ATH M-series, which, while being an excellent closed-back headphone series, feels like the sound is being pumped right into your brain. Because of this roominess, you'll experience better soundstage. You'll be able to hear not only the magnitude and tone of the sound, but also a more accurate representation of the spatial location of the sound, which is what makes it great for gaming and for listening to music with a lot of unique instruments, i.e., jazz, orchestral, etc. - The earpads are slightly larger than your normal over-ear headphone, but with good reason. Since your entire ear, or at least almost all of it, will naturally fit within it, less force is required to keep the phones positioned. As a result, these don't squeeze your brain like many studio phones do, and the fabric earpad material makes them comfortable to wear for hours at a time. The Less-than-perfect: - A downside one might experience with these is that they leak a good amount of sound out the back, but that's a characteristic of any open-back headphone. In return for the leakage, you get that excellent soundstage I mentioned earlier. Basically, don't plan on using these at work if you work in a quieter environment, because the leakage is noticeable to anyone sitting up to about 10 ft away. I use these as my home setup's primary headphones and they're quite perfect for the role. The Interesting: - The headband is a bit interesting, at least compared to the headphones I've used before. Instead of a traditional headband, these have pads attached to each can, as seen in the pictures, which gently squeeze your head to keep them positioned properly. Personally, I feel that the squeeze is just tight enough to keep the phones positioned comfortably. Some might think the hold is too loose, but that can easily be remedied by putting a rubber band around the pads to tighten the grip. Bottom Line: If you're looking for an outstanding, roomy-sounding, and comfortable headphone for your home setup, these are the cans for you. If you prefer to be more intimate and closer with your sound, look for closed-back cans.

Whatever people said about these headphones not being loud enough is, unfortunately, true. I though perhaps they were wrong, but no. I wish I believed them. I had them at max volume pretty much all the time. And yes, my volume was maxed out on the iPod/iPhone as well. The sound is very disappointing overall. Exaggerated mids and highs and weak low bass and almost no mid-bass. They completely lack any punch if you listen to electronic music or rock. I usually have my iPod EQ set to Electronic and that gives me satisfying sound with any headphones I ever used. With these headphones, at this EQ setting, the highs were so terribly exaggerated it was impossible to listen to anything. I had set the EQ to Bass Boost which gave me more bass and reduce the highs, but the sound was still weak. The SRS makes it even worse. SRS is a terrible gimmick. If you make a quality gear there is no need for gimmicky sound processing. In my opinion SRS just destroyed already weak sound by increasing already exaggerated highs and scrambling already weak bass. I was very, very disappointed. I expected much better for $300. Noise canceling (NC) is also very underwehelming. When turned on, it makes the sound even worse, even quieter and flatter with almost no bass. My 5+ year old SONY wired NC headphones do much better job at noise canceling and produce more powerful sound and they were around $130 when I bough them years ago. Again, I expected much better from the latest technology for $300. BT doesn't add that much to the cost. Also, NC introduces weird audio artifacts. It's hard to explain but the sound is really, really weird with the NC on, like kind of reverse stereo, polarized sound, I don't know what to describe it, my old SONY headphones don't do that. On top of that, when there are sudden, loud low frequency noises, such as when the bus hits a bump, the electronics completely freak out and create loud, unpleasant thumping and fluttering counter-sound, which is unbearable after a while. I ended up not using noise canceling, it was that bad. Again, my old SONYs don't do that, unless the sound is really loud, like being passed by a big truck few feet away. These Sennheisers just can't handle any loud sounds. Without NC, they don't provide enough isolation. They do a passable job without NC indoors, in a quiet environment comparable to any average headphones that sell for quarter of the price. But due to the poor electronics and weak sound they are useless as noise canceling headphones in any real life, noisy situation. The cups are too small, both the circumference and the depth. I don't have big ears. I never had this problem with any other over-the-ear headphones. This is the first time. These squeeze or pinch my earlobes, there simply isn't enough room inside the cups. I found myself constantly repositioning the headphones to relieve pressure on my earlobes. There simply isn't anything positive I can say about this product. Weak sound, poor noise canceling and uncomfortable cups add up for pretty lousy experience. Considering the price I was unable to justify keeping them. They've gone back. Anyone who describes these headphones as having "great bass" simply doesn't listen to music that contains deep, punchy bass. Bass response of these headphones combined with low volume and inefficient noise canceling is simply weak.

If you want the best possible sound quality Bluetooth headsets, get an AudioTechnica AT-PH05BT - a standalone Bluetooth headphone receiver/amp. Add to that a better headset. If you like Sony, I like the MDR7506 A LOT. Sadly the AT-PH05BT is only sold in Japan, but you can order it via Amazon (see my review on how to use it). But back to reality... Do not be misled by Amazon: the MDR10RBT IS NOT A NEWER MODEL OF THESE. Sony still makes these and quite honestly there's really no comparison. I can tolerate the MDR10RBTS for certain kinds of light classical music, but only when I don't have these with me. These still are not perfect-enough sounding to rate 5 stars. These are quite comfortable; the sound stage is just about right; frequency response is too bass-heavy (worth 1 start deduction), but not excessively so; the sound quality (other than the bass) is quite good on what I've heard so far via internet radio w/Bluetooth (Verdi Requiem, #4 of Richard Strauss's 4 last songs and J. S. Bach cantata BWV 35). The large orchestras sound like the hall is too live (bass again); the vocals are crystal clear and quite beautiful; the organ and harpsichord (a tad unusual in combination) are excellent (organ is one of the few places where extra bass is almost good). The sound is involving, but not riveting (see my review of Shure SRH-840 (wired) - those are riveting). Not being riveting is not a bad thing if you're trying to listen and do other things at the same time. The JVC HARX900s (wired) are also good in that regard. Bluetooth reception and signal processing are excellent. Even on Bluetooth, the sound is not fatiguing (modulo bass again). Because of the cleanliness of sound there's a temptation to play them too loudly. All cans are fatiguing when they're to loud for too long. The documentation shows 2 different audio cables. Mine only came with one (as did my MDR10RBTs): the regular 3.5mm TRS sound one. The mic/phone cable (with TRRS connectors (two rings)) was not present. Despite warnings to the contrary, any high quality cable with 3.5mm TRS connectors (one ring) will work OK for regular listening use. I use my Shure SRH840s for critical listening and my AKG k240s for casual listening (or my JVC HARX900s for even more casual listening). These are an acceptable wireless alternative. They're pretty bulky to carry around (other on one's head): they only fold flat; the don't collapse. I also replaced their nice-but-a-tad-tight pouch with a large GoodCans one. I use this one's pouch for my mdr10rbts, which come in a pouch that's way too small. Bottom line: They're steep, but not out of line and for Bluetooth headsets (without an intermediate device) you can't do better.

You can see in the pictures that I figured out to to make the Plus stay in my ears. I purchased an anti-loss strap from WOFRO. It came as shown in the second picture- and I didn't like it at all. The cord is stiff rubber. It caught in my hair and stuck to my shoulders when I turned my head. Also, with noise cancellation and ambient sound controls, you never really need to take these out of your ears. So I cut the cords off the skin that holds the buds- and IT'S PERFECT! The skin is so thin they fit in the charging base. It's just enough rubber to create traction and keep them in my ears. Also, the charging case works perfectly with them. It took a couple of tries to get them on - you need to avoid all the contact points. Just take your time and you'll be happy you tried this. For me, the Pro offers superior noise cancellation and great sound. And now they stay in my ears. I'm keeping this pair!

I had some version of these in my cart for almost a year before I finally bought a pair. I wish I had done it earlier; for the price, these are delightful. Comfort--soft, not too tight, and I generally fall asleep wearing them, even though I'm a side-sleeper. I have used them much more often than I thought I would. Privacy--If you plan to share a bed (or airplane row, or whatever) with someone, there's no sound leakage that I can detect. Price--when I bought these, they were hovering around the 20 dollar range. Which means I can sleep in them without freaking out about losing or damaging a substantial investment. Durability--I toss and turn in my sleep; these so far stay on and undamaged despite my thrashing. Cons: Battery--these need to be charged daily. Full stop. They seem to *hold* a charge pretty well, but if you sleep in them, as I do, you're not going to get more than one night out of a charge. The only reason I gave a four rather than a five star review is that the battery seems a little weak, and the "LOW BATTERY" voice is a bit alarming. Hair--I pull this over my head and then push it back up, like a hairband. If you wear it as some of the pictures show, you're gonna get some weird bedhead. But if you shower in the morning, who cares? These do exactly what I hoped they would, but they do it a little better than I thought they would. At this price point, I'd say get 'em.

Got these for my many flights. Noise cancelling is simply excellent. If combined with ear plugs I cannot imagine what would wake you up. Music and sound books sound great to me but I'm no audiofile others may differ. Because these are closed to keep out noise I get hot around my ears on longer trips and wake up with "sweaty" ears. Not a big deal for me but may be good to know before you buy. I do not think they feel flimsy but I have not had them long enough to say anything about their life span. On the other hand I can say this; if they serve me well for 2 years I will consider it a good purchase, as heavy travel does tend to wear down things faster than at home. One star off for the somewhat high price (even if I do not see any real competition at this price point). UPDATE: Thought I had lost these and bought the Bose QC3 in stead. So now I can compare the two main Bose models directly. Noise cancelling effect: Noise cancelling system is equally effective on both models. However, the closed design of the QC15 give them a slight advantage when it comes to sheer noise blocking (not all noises are handled by the noise cancelling system). Music: No difference to me. But as mentioned above I not an audiophile and I spend far most time listening to audio books anyway. Comfort: This is probably what people should choose after between the two. QC15 cannot escape the fact they are bulky + closed design may give you "sweaty" ears as mentioned above. However, I personally still prefer QC15 because my ears are quite sensitive to presure and I cannot have the QC3 mounted for a long distance flight (5 hours+) without resting my ears once in a while. Not doubt that QC3 are easier to sleep with due to less bulk if you have a custom shaped pillow (I always bring one with a special "dip" for the earphones). Operation: Same cord system and built-in remote iphone/ipad control. However, the battery system is distinctly different. The QC15 takes standard batteries while the QC3 relies on a special battery unit you have to charge. The special battery on the QC3 saves weight and lasts for 15 hours (also in real life use). However, the draw down is of course the need for a charger, special battery and for charging. As I do gruelling 30 hour+ flights this is an issue. Some people buy an extra battery for their QC3. Recommended if you travel a lot but it adds even more to the extra price for the QC3. Travel size/weight: In-box the size difference is too small to matter. The QC3 box is smaller, but not by much. The QC15 case is actually more neat on the inside because there are fewer parts to go around and the QC3 box design seems less well thought out. QC3 is lighter and you can feel the difference. Conclusion: Get the pair that fits your ears - I deeply regretted getting the QC3 instead and am very happy that I have my QC15 back - but YMMV and QC3 may be the better choice for others.
